title: What the Iraq War Foretold About How the Iran War Will End
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Last week, Democrats dominated elections as Donald Trump, a lame-duck Republican, waged an unpopular war in Iran that he started and that a majority of Americans want to end
Notice the parallels to 20 years ago: In 2006, Democrats dominated the midterms as George W
Bush, a lame-duck Republican, waged an unpopular war in Iraq that he chose to start and that a majority of Americans wanted to end
Back then, with Democrats in control of both chambers of Congress for the first time in 12 years, The Atlantic asked 44 foreign-policy specialists about withdrawal from Iraq
Most people surveyed for this 2007 article predicted that policy would move in the direction that voters wanted: an end to the war
Around that time, 130,000 to 150,000 U.S. troops were in Iraq
Seventy-three percent of respondents said that America would not have a significant military presence in Iraq (defined as 50,000 troops or more) five years in the future
And they were correct––although that oversimplifies what came next
Revisiting what happened with regard to Iraq is a helpful reminder that winning elections by campaigning against a war is far easier than actually ending the conflict

In January 2007, days after the Democratic-majority Congress was sworn in, Bush gave the anti-war coalition the opposite of what it wanted: He told the public that he had already begun “the surge,” which would increase U.S. troop levels in Iraq to roughly 170,000
Democrats in the House passed a nonbinding resolution disapproving of the policy
Nearly two months later, they passed a $124 billion emergency spending bill for Iraq and Afghanistan, which also mandated that within months the United States would start pulling troops out of Iraq
But Bush vetoed the bill , arguing that “setting a deadline for withdrawal is setting a date for failure,” and that the U.S. should not tell enemies its plans
That December , under pressure to support the troops, Congress approved $70 billion in additional funding for Iraq and Afghanistan
The following year, as conditions in Iraq improved, Bush began reducing America’s military presence and handing security matters over to the Iraqis
Barack Obama, who had campaigned on ending the “dumb war,” won the White House and continued winding down military activity
By 2012, nearly all U.S. forces were gone—but that didn’t last
Obama ended up redeploying troops to Iraq in 2014 to respond to the rise of the Islamic State
President Trump, who also criticized the war in his 2016 campaign, kept soldiers there to continue fighting ISIS
Not until his second term, earlier this year, did the final withdrawal of U.S. forces occur
All told, America’s military stayed in Iraq for years under multiple Congresses and presidents who won elections by appealing to voters who wanted the war to be over

The Atlantic asked the foreign-policy experts one other question back in 2007: How should the United States withdraw from Iraq? The most popular answer (46 percent) urged a phased withdrawal to minimize chaos; the least popular answer (5 percent) favored an “immediate, full-scale withdrawal.” Today, most Americans want the war in Iran to end , but how it should end is less certain

Here the Iraq withdrawal ceases to be a close parallel: America seems less able to dictate events in Iran, because that war is being waged against an intact regime, rather than against insurgents after a military victory, and Iran’s ability to challenge American interests––by closing the Strait of Hormuz, attacking American military bases, and striking U.S. allies in the region––could complicate plans
Plus, America’s enemies in Iraq did not have the capacity to develop a nuclear weapon in 2006

Iran’s ability to go nuclear is contested, and if it obtained “a nuclear weapon during my term,” Trump told 60 Minutes over the weekend, “I would be excoriated far worse than what’s happened.” He may be right
As much as Americans want the war to conclude, they also overwhelmingly agree that Iran should not possess such a weapon
But Trump’s statement elides confident claims he made last year about bygone missile strikes destroying Iran’s nuclear capabilities, undermining his own public rationale for war
Come January, America will once again have a Republican president who maintains that he made the right call by going to war and a congressional majority under pressure to end the war
If Trump presses ahead, knowing he’ll never face voters again, Congress could stop him if it is willing to cut off military funding for Iran operations

But do Democrats have the votes to do so and the willingness to live with the results? As in 2006, lawmakers tend to hesitate when foreseeing potential political risks—in this case, being blamed for an American loss or a nuclear Iran
Instead, they may be tempted to take measures short of actually forcing Trump’s hand
Already in June, the Republican-controlled Congress passed a bipartisan resolution telling Trump to get congressional approval to continue the war or to withdraw the military from Iran
When he ignored the legislation, lawmakers let him keep fighting anyway without consequence
Trump has since acknowledged that the war helped Democrats win the House and the Senate, and said that he expects the conflict to end soon

But today, in announcing that Vance, an Iran-war skeptic, will no longer take part in negotiations, Trump seemed to abandon the idea of a diplomatic resolution. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he wrote on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” It seems possible that Americans will be clashing over Iran policy for years to come
The history of the Iraq War suggests that, even when voters want peace, finishing conflicts that a president favors is far harder than starting them
Related: Trump could leave the Iran mess to his successor
The U.S. and Iran are fighting a massively asymmetrical war

title: The Jensen Huang Scandal Should Change Everything
excerpt: Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia, following revelations of an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chin
body: Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia, following revelations of an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese-intelligence asset, should force a fundamental rethinking of America’s AI strategy
Jensen Huang was not just the CEO of the world’s most important semiconductor company
He was also one of Donald Trump’s closest and most influential advisers on AI
Huang persuaded Trump to abandon his initial embrace of export controls, arguing that U.S. technology firms should compete in China
He persistently argued that AI is more akin to electricity than a weapon and that warnings about AI safety were wildly overblown—a view that Trump fully internalized
In the coming months, Congress will scrutinize every aspect of the scandal

Among these are the Commerce Department’s suspension of its investigation into Megaspeed, the Singaporean company that Alice Huang was a director of; the failure to crack down on China’s extensive chip-smuggling operation in Southeast Asia; Nvidia’s financial contributions to Trump’s pet projects, such as the White House ballroom; and China’s possible illicit influence over other business leaders in America. [ Read: A $5.7 trillion face-plant ] The scandal comes at a moment of deep national dissatisfaction and anxiety about AI, and it is likely to reinforce public concerns that the companies developing this technology are given too much influence over how it is governed
In the recent midterm elections, candidates promising restrictions on data-center construction made significant gains

Dario Amodei and Sam Altman , the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI, respectively, have warned that new models could come with tremendous risk and suggested that the companies should “pace the frontier.” Hardly a week passes without news of unprecedented cyberattacks, some of which are powered by AI
In July, for example, autonomous agents undergoing safety testing at OpenAI escaped their sandbox and hacked into the systems of Hugging Face, another AI company
America’s conundrum is this: The United States must stay ahead of China, but it also has to take safety seriously
The answer is not to accelerate development or to seek a grand bargain with Beijing, but to strengthen export controls
Stronger controls will help preserve America’s lead, creating the room to slow down development and ensure that new models are rigorously tested before they are released
Winning the race with China has become a one-size-fits-all excuse for business executives to advance their company’s interests and reject calls for regulation of any kind
Politicians have also fallen into this trap

In September, Senator Ted Cruz told Politico , “If they’re going to be killer robots, I’d rather they be American killer robots and not Chinese killer robots.” Geopolitics are a poor excuse for doing something irrational
But to say , as Huang did, that who wins the race doesn’t really matter is equally wrong
In April, Anthropic announced that it had developed a model called Mythos, which gave users extremely advanced cyberattack capabilities

Rather than releasing Mythos to the public, Anthropic worked with the Trump administration to set up Project Glasswing, which gave the top U.S. companies access to the model for cyberdefense, so that they could plug their gaps as quickly as possible
If China or any other state had developed Mythos-like capabilities first, it would not likely have shared the model with U.S. companies, which would have been left exposed
Several senators have proposed a tempting solution: The United States should negotiate a comprehensive arms control with China to pause or slow down AI development
Altman has said that such a deal would be easy for Trump and Xi Jinping to agree to
Verification would be extremely difficult
China would likely see the pursuit of such an agreement as a U.S. attempt to lock in a lead
In a recent statement , the head of the Ministry for State Security, China’s intelligence services, made clear that China sees AI competition with the United States in adversarial terms
That doesn’t rule out talks and coordinated actions to address specific safety risks, but it does mean that a grand bargain is extremely unlikely
Taking safety seriously is impossible if the AI developers continue at full throttle
The models are close to being able to improve themselves, a capacity that could dramatically accelerate technological progress beyond the ability of humans to evaluate and control it
That’s why the United States needs to strengthen its export controls and double down on safety in the lead time that gives it over China
Although China is working hard to develop its indigenous chip-manufacturing capability, it is still struggling
In June 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testified to Congress that China produces only about 200,000 advanced chips annually, a tiny number compared with what it needs
Chips are the one advantage that the United States has over China, and Washington needs to capitalize on this
Much of China’s progress appears to have depended on access to American AI models
Chinese companies have used distillation, a technique whereby a less capable model is trained by a more powerful one, allowing it to duplicate some of those capabilities quickly

In February, Anthropic revealed that DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax had generated more than 16 million exchanges with Claude through approximately 24,000 fraudulent accounts to extract its capabilities
The company later uncovered an even larger operation by Alibaba, involving more than 150 million exchanges designed to improve its Qwen models
In September, the FBI and the NSA warned that Chinese laboratories were using large-scale distillation to acquire American AI capabilities at a fraction of the cost of developing them independently
As we now know from the Nvidia scandal, espionage also likely plays a role
Huang knew more than any other individual about who was getting advanced chips
Access to that information could have proved invaluable to a foreign actor

title: An Offbeat Director Worth Your Time
excerpt: Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession
body: Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession
This week marks the limited-theater release of Paper Tiger , a muted, tragic crime thriller that’s the latest film in the director James Gray’s heady oeuvre

The story, set in Brooklyn and Queens in the 1980s, manages to be both tightly focused and operatic in scale: Two brothers (played by Adam Driver and Miles Teller) get in over their heads on a business scheme, and must watch as their dream of climbing the social ladder is brutally ripped away—partly thanks to their own mistakes
This tale of relatably flawed people is, in my opinion, one of the year’s must-see films, which is true basically anytime Gray makes a movie
And yet, so many cinemagoers still seem to have never heard of him

That lack of awareness could be partly because only a couple of his films could reasonably be called hits—the 2007 cop thriller We Own the Night was a solid performer, and his sci-fi epic, Ad Astra , did reasonable (if unspectacular) business in 2019

Big-name actors like working with Gray, including Joaquin Phoenix, Brad Pitt, Mark Wahlberg, and Scarlett Johansson, who co-stars in Paper Tiger ; their eager participation helps him secure $15 million budgets
But his films are usually dark affairs that don’t leave the audience with easy answers or tidy lessons learned
Most of them take place in outer-borough New York; many are period pieces
Yet Gray often finds a way to tell these stories on the margins through seemingly glitzy trappings

In Paper Tiger , the characters’ entire story arcs might amount to a two-minute conversation you hear in the background of a much grander mob movie: Driver plays Gary Pearl, a former cop who has become a showboat of a private-security consultant, while Teller is his industrious brother, Irwin, an engineer who’s married to Hester (Johansson) with two teenage kids

Gary talks Irwin into going into business with him helping to clean up an industrial lot in Brooklyn’s polluted Gowanus Canal, promising big money in return; quickly, it becomes clear that they are working with the Russian mob, and Irwin’s attention to detail is perceived by the gangsters as untoward snooping
From there, Gary and Irwin’s illusions of professional safety quickly vanish
The dreadful violence and recrimination that follow feels both completely avoidable and utterly inevitable
That tension is what defines so many of Gray’s films—some Shakespearean drama happening on a prosaic, human level

The violence is always shocking and narratively earned, while still feeling intensely cinematic (there’s a shoot-out sequence near the end of Paper Tiger that is one of the coolest action sequences I’ve seen in a movie all year)

We Own the Night has an incredible car chase that echoes classics of the genre, such as The French Connection ; Ad Astra features a thrilling set piece involving moon-buggy warfare unlike anything I’d ever seen staged in a sci-fi movie
Yet both of those films are also about the kind of interpersonal drama a friend might tell you about over a long night of drinking at a bar
No matter what the setting, Gray homes in on the most understandable sorts of failure

The excellent Two Lovers is a tragicomic romance, starring Joaquin Phoenix and Gwyneth Paltrow, that transposes the tale of a Dostoyevsky character (inspired by the story “White Nights”) to modern-day Brighton Beach, in Brooklyn

Another tale of the sort is The Lost City of Z , an adaptation of David Grann’s fantastic nonfiction work about the explorer Percy Fawcett, who vanished deep in the Amazon while looking for evidence of ancient civilization
These are fatally flawed protagonists, heroes as likely to be felled by family trauma as by grandiose ambition
Paper Tiger is one of Gray’s best movies, and it’s attracting rave reviews
Yet I worry it’s going to go the same route as most of his filmography—highly praised, with underwhelming ticket sales and little awards attention
The film played at the Cannes Film Festival, where Gray’s work has been in competition six times without ever winning an award (even he seems sick of going there )
He’s received zero Oscar nominations over the course of a storied career
It’s hard to put a finger on why; perhaps his work is too minor-key for voting bodies
Obviously, the biggest win for any director is getting to make more movies, and I think Gray will continue to do that without much issue—great actors always seem to want to collaborate with him
But a film like Paper Tiger deserves to be seen widely; go if you can, and you’ll soon want to delve into the rest of Gray’s fascinating, knotty filmography

An Essay I Enjoyed Illustration by Alisa Gao / The Atlantic The Unbearable Mediocrity of Microdramas By Elise Hannum For one weekend in October, the AMC theater off of New York City’s Union Square wasn’t playing any recognizable new releases

Instead, it was closed to the general public, with the sidewalk outside taken over by a small red carpet covered by a white tent, where the occasional group of attractive actor types in suits and gowns got their photo taken
Inside, the bar offered a promotional cocktail; a merch stand downstairs sold exclusive baseball caps and tote bags
The attendees were there to watch screenings, but not of traditional wide-screen features: These films took up only a sliver of the screen, with a five-foot black space on either side
Coming Attractions Until this week, James Gunn and Peter Safran, the co-heads of DC Studios, seemed to have no reason to fear for their jobs
Clayface , the latest installment in the comic-book movie franchise, was a mild success at the box office; they seemed to have made it through the huge post–Warner Bros.–Paramount merger unscathed
Well, no more: Skydance, as that new company is called, announced on Monday that Gunn and Safran were exiting the company, just four years after taking the roles
On the one hand, I’m sad to see them go, as their creative perspective came across as quite exciting and not so ruthlessly corporate
Releasing an adaptation of Clayface before introducing the franchise’s take on Batman is wacky, yet the end result was a pretty fun bit of gory horror that did decent business

On the other hand, as I noted in a previous edition of the newsletter, that movie did next to nothing to advance any wider stories—ostensibly the goal for an interconnected series that tends to receive two or three big new installments a year

And while Gunn and Safran also had a couple of other projects in the pipeline (including the Gunn-directed Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow , in theaters next summer), their rollout of the new DC universe had been arguably plodding

title: Investigating Michel Houellebecq Is a Dangerous Mistake
excerpt: An assault on free speech is unfolding in France
body: An assault on free speech is unfolding in France

On Tuesday, a judge placed Michel Houellebecq, one of the country’s most significant living writers, under investigation for his alleged “complicity in incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence,” an accusation that stems from comments he made about Muslims several years ago
Houellebecq’s remarks were controversial and insensitive, but defending his freedom to speak does not require finding his words unobjectionable
Even the most offensive generalizations about minority groups should have to meet an exceptionally high threshold to warrant such a legal intervention
The fact that he now faces the possibility of criminal charges should concern anyone who professes to care about the free exchange of ideas

Houellebecq’s supposed crime occurred in November 2022 during an interview with the magazine Front Populaire . “When entire territories come under Islamist control, I think acts of resistance will take place,” Houellebecq said. “There will be attacks and shootings in mosques, in cafés frequented by Muslims, in short, Bataclans in reverse.” He was referring to a 2015 attack on Paris’s Bataclan concert hall, one of several acts of jihadist terrorism in the 2010s that collectively killed hundreds in France. “I believe that the wish of the population with French roots, as the phrase goes, is not for Muslims to assimilate,” Houellebecq continued, “but for them to stop stealing from and assaulting them, in short, for the violence to decrease, for them to respect the law and people

Or, another good solution, for them to leave.” [ Thomas Chatterton Williams: The violence sweeping France was never really about schools ] Elsewhere in the interview, Houellebecq spoke about the “Great Replacement.” This idea, coined by the French writer Renaud Camus , casts demographic change through immigration as the replacement of native European populations, particularly by Muslims. “I was very shocked that it was called a theory
It’s not a theory, it’s a fact,” Houellebecq said
Camus “observed a great replacement or—to be more precise—the changing ethnic and religious composition of the European population

It is statistically evident.” Houellebecq’s lawyers have disputed that his remarks amount to incitement, correctly noting that predicting violence is not the same as provoking it. “The incriminated remarks have no dimension of incitement, not even implicitly, and therefore fall within the bounds of freedom of opinion and expression,” they said in a statement to the French media. “A prophet of doom does not wish for disaster, quite the contrary
His place is not in a courtroom.” After the interview came out, Muslim and anti-racist groups filed complaints against Houellebecq
In 2023, he published a memoir that described his comments as clumsy, an obvious and somewhat lame attempt at self-preservation
If the book was a ploy to eliminate his legal exposure, it didn’t work
Multiple groups declined to withdraw their complaints, which ultimately led to the investigation announced this week
The debate over Houellebecq’s comments acquired renewed urgency following a mass shooting last month

On October 23, a 39-year-old gunman drove through the communes of Trappes and La Verrière, outside Paris, and fired a submachine gun at passersby whom he believed to be African or Muslim, according to prosecutors
He killed a 26-year-old man of African descent and injured seven others, including an 11-year-old girl
Investigators found a copy of Mein Kampf in his home
Yesterday, the Union of Mosques of France, one of the groups that had filed a complaint against Houellebecq, issued a statement invoking the attack as an illustration of the danger of his rhetoric

But no matter how deplorable the attack was, it doesn’t erase the crucial distinction between foreseeing violence and inciting it; a plain reading of Houellebecq’s words shows that he was engaged in the former
France does not guarantee the same speech protections that Americans take for granted under the First Amendment
In the United States, the legal standard for incitement holds that speech must be aimed at producing imminent unlawful action, and is likely to produce it
In France, the standard is lower: Incitement may be punishable even if it’s merely implicit , its intended effect isn’t imminent, and it’s unlikely to have any effect whatsoever
All manner of verbal transgressions have resulted in convictions, fines, and even time in jail
In 2011, for example, a Paris court convicted the designer John Galliano of making racist and anti-Semitic insults in public
In Houellebecq’s case, the language used by the judge is telling
The allegation concerns the incitement of “discrimination, hatred, or violence,” three terms with radically different meanings
Punishing speech that is intended and likely to provoke imminent violence is one thing
But criminalizing the encouragement of something so nebulous as “hatred” of a group is far too broad a power to grant the state
And the allegation comes years after the fact
How far back can a causal chain reach? This isn’t the first time that Houellebecq has faced legal trouble for comments he made about Muslims
In 2002, he was prosecuted after referring to Islam in an interview as “the stupidest religion.” He was later acquitted, but the investigation was itself a penalty
The prospect of being subjected to such cumbersome proceedings, which can last years, preemptively chills speech
Right-wing American politicians such as J
Vance have scolded Europeans for taking such an authoritarian approach to wrongthink
They are hypocrites, given their own administration’s offenses

But they are nonetheless correct. [ Read: Europe’s free-speech problem ] The point is not whether Houellebecq said anything objectionable, but that we all ought to retain the right to express objectionable views
Immigration, demographic change, and the reality of Islamist violence are issues that France cannot wish away
Indeed, they are pressing political concerns and must remain subjects open to candid disagreement
That includes arguments that may be exaggerated, offensive, or wrong

title: Why Black Voters Abandoned Trump
excerpt: E arly in 2024 , Donald Trump took the stage at the Black Conservative Federation gala in South Carolina. “We love you!” one audience member yelled. “We love yo
body: E arly in 2024 , Donald Trump took the stage at the Black Conservative Federation gala in South Carolina. “We love you!” one audience member yelled. “We love you,” Trump responded , adding, “We’ve energized the Republican Party, and we’ve expanded the Republican Party.” At the time, he was right: The share of Black voters supporting Trump had ticked up in 2020 and seemed to be growing. “And they’re going, Wait a minute—there must be a mistake here ; they’re saying, Black people must really like Trump

As he looked around at the organization’s leaders onstage with him, he smiled and said, “These guys know it’s no mistake.” When ballots were cast later that year, roughly 15 percent of Black voters chose Trump over Kamala Harris in the general election, up from 6 percent in 2016 and 8 percent in 2020, according to the Pew Research Center
The gains were mainly among Black men, about 21 percent of whom took a flier on Trump, according to exit polling

Theories for the shift abounded: The culprit was misogyny, or frustration with President Biden and the Democratic Party in general, or the lure of rhetoric about strong families and self-reliance, or the appeal of Trump’s bravado to otherwise-disempowered young men
No one argument could capture the full picture, but the bottom line was clear: Black voters seemed to be moving, however tentatively, toward Trump and the GOP
Two years later, the picture looks different
According to the Associated Press , about 90 percent of Black voters supported Democrats last Tuesday, up from the roughly eight in 10 who went for Harris in 2024
Strong turnout throughout the country—and especially in majority-minority counties in the South—helped secure historic wins for Democrats

In Georgia, where Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman to be elected governor of any U.S. state, the share of Black midterm voters who went to the polls last week reached 54 percent , up from 45.5 percent in 2022 and 39 percent in 2010
In Texas, where a blue wave swept the entire slate of Democrats into statewide office for the first time in decades, the early and absentee Black vote rose 53 percent from 2022

And in Mississippi, where Scott Colom displaced the Republican incumbent to become the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, Black voters made up 33 percent of the electorate, up from 30 percent in 2024

Only about one in 10 Black men voted for the Republican on the ballot—except in Florida, where about a quarter of Black men and 10 percent of Black women backed the GOP candidate, Byron Donalds, making him the state’s first Black governor

The question now is whether last Tuesday’s vote proves that 2024 was an anomaly and that Black voters have come back to the Democratic Party to stay, or whether they will be up for grabs in 2028 and beyond

Christopher Towler, a political scientist at California State University at Sacramento who studies Black voting behavior, argues that the shift toward Trump in 2024 was never as significant as it appeared, and that much of it could be explained by diminished overall turnout among Black voters that year. “Turnout influences how we interpret these partisan supports,” Towler told me

He said the share of Black voters who choose Republicans has stayed relatively stable for six decades (except for 1996 and 2008, when nearly all Black voters backed the Democrat for president), but it accounts for a larger percentage of the Black vote in low-turnout elections
Towler never bought the idea that the 2024 election marked the start of a racial realignment in politics. “All the evidence has suggested that is absolutely not the case,” he said
Instead, that spike in Black support for Trump more likely reflected who showed up and who stayed home
But for Democratic operatives, the 2024 numbers should still ring some alarm bells
Charles Coleman Jr., a civil-rights lawyer and political analyst, told me fluctuations in turnout reflect a paradigm shift in how Black Americans participate in politics
Black voters have always been pragmatic: They vote for the party that they believe will “do us less harm,” he said
But this has been changing. “There are more and more members of the Black electorate who are tired of a ‘less harm’ orientation,” he said

They “want proactive policy that is going to benefit them.” If they don’t get it, they may just stay home. [ Madeleine Carlisle and Russell Berman: Republicans redistricted themselves out of Congress ] In practice, this means that Democrats can no longer assume that being the least-bad party will energize Black voters
The confluence of events that catalyzed a surge in Black turnout this year cannot be counted on to boost voter rolls in the next election or the one after that
Any party seeking to either keep Black voters in the fold or woo them to their camp will have to offer more than promises
B lack voters have grown accustomed to an insulting routine: When election season rolls around, candidates go to Black churches and barbershops to make their pitch and show voters that they care
This can make Black people feel like props , glad-handed just in time for their votes

Garlin Gilchrist, a Democrat and Michigan’s first Black lieutenant governor, who was just elected Michigan’s secretary of state, told me that he traveled to every one of Michigan’s 83 counties at least three times. “I try to model consistency
I’m here with you, talking to you, listening to you, understanding what’s going on,” he said

But he noticed in his tours that many Black voters had grown jaded. “What I see are people who are just like, I’m sick of running in place, I’m sick of these people lying, I’m sick of these prices going up, and I’m sick of people acting like I only matter sometimes ,” he said last week, not long after he cast his ballot

Johnson, a Democrat, signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which banned racial segregation in public places and outlawed employment discrimination, Black voters have been the Democratic Party’s most reliable bloc

The “southern strategy” embraced by the Republican Party in the 1960s, which saw politicians play to the prejudices of white voters across the region, transformed the southern political landscape and alienated Black voters
For decades, the political calculus for Black voters had been clear: The Democrats are the “less harm” party
But a choice between empty promises and outright bigotry is hardly a choice at all
While campaigning amid the coronavirus pandemic and the racial reckoning of 2020, Biden made a number of commitments to appeal to Black people
As he had promised, he tapped a Black woman for vice president and appointed the first Black woman to the Supreme Court
He also made Juneteenth a federal holiday and fought racial discrimination in the housing market
But Black voters began souring on him after his first year in office, disappointed by the failure of Democrats to pass key voting-rights legislation, and later by rising prices
By May 2024, pundits warn ed that Black voters were starting to splinter off from the Democratic coalition

Over the past decade, the share of Black Americans who identify as Democrats has fallen, from 65 percent in 2013 to 49 percent in 2025, whereas the shares of those who identify as independent, Republican, or “other” have all risen
The share of “other” Black voters grew the most, from 7 percent in 2013 to 18 percent last year

title: Scott Colom Is Mississippi’s First Black Senator in 150 Years
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white Democratic former congressman and state legislator named E
Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote
An all-white jury accepted Hurst’s claim that he had acted in self-defense because Lee came at him with a tire iron
Donald Trump, now the sitting president of the United States, was 15 years old
This was how “negro law” worked in Jim Crow Mississippi, which was essentially a police state

Although many laws were race-neutral in their language, “in a society in which race mattered above all else, ‘negro law’ determined who was punished for what,” the historian Neil McMillen wrote in Dark Journey , his 1989 history of Mississippi

In the 1940s, the NAACP was “virtually forced to operate underground,” because in 1920, the state legislature had made it illegal to “possess or distribute” material that would “disturb relations between the races.” As late as 1961, a white man could shoot a Black man in broad daylight and get away with it

When the Black reporter Simeon Booker arrived in 1955 to cover the lynching of Emmett Till for Jet magazine, he wrote that he witnessed “not only raw hatred, but state condoned terror.” This apparatus of state-condoned terror was still active into the 1960s

As Thomas Ricks writes in Waging a Good War , his history of the civil-rights movement as a nonviolent military campaign, when the legendary civil-rights organizer Bob Moses went down to Mississippi he was “assaulted and jailed repeatedly, sometimes simply for speaking to white people as equals.” In 1963, Moses and other organizers survived a drive-by shooting

He later wrote to the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee that Mississippi was extremely dangerous—“we were just like sitting ducks” and “people were just going to be wiped out.” [ Adam Serwer: Even where MAGA won, MAGA lost ] The point of all this terror was to prevent what happened yesterday, when the Democrat Scott Colom defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction
Hyde-Smith attended a segregation academy as a child—private schools set up in the South to circumvent the Brown v
Board of Education ruling to integrate public schools
She had previously blocked Colom’s appointment to the federal bench
On Election Night, Hyde-Smith declared victory , saying, “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a U.S
Senator.” That was a little premature. “In Mississippi, our prayers often change the course of history,” Colom said in his victory speech last night. “It’s not something that I did, y’all

All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this.” The last Black man to have served as a U.S. senator from Mississippi, Blanche Bruce—back then senators were appointed by the state legislature—was born enslaved in 1841
His mother was enslaved, and his father was her master in the eyes of the law

One of Bruce’s votes was against the Republican-supported Chinese Exclusion Act, which he explained as a vote of conscience and solidarity, “representing as I do a people who are considered essentially disqualified from the privileges and immunities of American citizenship.” Before the turn of the 20th century, Mississippi was majority-Black
State-tolerated (or state-encouraged) terror led many Black Mississippians to flee north during the Great Migration
Today, Mississippi still has the highest proportion of Black residents of any state

Before the Voting Rights Act was passed in 1965, law and violence kept Black Mississippians disenfranchised; after, racially polarized voting would place a hard ceiling on the aspirations of every Black candidate in this red state

The last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate was John Stennis, an avowed segregationist who, as a prosecutor in the 1930s, led the prosecution of three Black men who had been tortured into confessions, a case that led the Supreme Court to rule in 1936 that such confessions are inadmissible under the Fourteenth Amendment
This is all to say, as one famous Mississippian put it, that “the past is never dead
It’s not even past.” Mississippi today is not the Mississippi of Dark Journey , but we are living in a world inextricably shaped by it
Multiracial democracy in America is young; it emerged only in the lifetimes of the people who are still currently governing the country
It is younger than most of the justices on the Supreme Court
The past decade has seen a relentless attack on its foundations from people who remember the time before multiracial democracy as a golden age
It was not a golden age in Mississippi, not for people like Herbert Lee, or Bob Moses, or Fannie Lou Hamer
Conservatives have undone or undermined many of the laws and constitutional amendments passed to ensure that Black Americans could exercise their rights as full citizens
The Supreme Court has slowly chipped away at the Voting Rights Act, most recently ruling in Louisiana v
Callais that racist voting restrictions are constitutional if they are passed with partisan, rather than racist, intent
This standard would permit many Jim Crow–era laws that were superficially race-neutral but racist in intent

As McMillen observed, in pre-1965 Mississippi, “Much of the exclusionary process was necessarily left to the discriminatory application of otherwise racially neutral law.” (If lawmakers want to disenfranchise Democratic voters, and those voters just happen to be Black—by coincidence, of course!—that’s fine.) Many Republican-controlled states in the South responded to the ruling by gerrymandering Black-majority districts out of existence

At the time, the former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale gleefully speculated that “if states are aggressive, we could see a healthy majority in the House perpetually.” Republicans might never have to worry about courting Black voters again
Black Americans responded to this assault on the foundations of their freedom with terrific fervor in the midterms
Black-voter turnout in the South appears to have surged last week to a hair below levels usually seen when a president is on the ballot

That, along with increased white support for Democrats, helped put previously deep-red states like Mississippi into contention. [ Adam Serwer: Texas Republicans get washed ] The next Congress will have seven Black U.S. senators—Colom, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Tim Scott of South Carolina, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Cory Booker of New Jersey—the most ever in history

There will be five contemporaneous Black governors in the United States in 2027, with Wes Moore in Maryland, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Byron Donalds in Florida, David Crowley in Wisconsin, and Aaron Ford in Nevada
Before this election, there had been only three such elected governors: Moore, Douglas Wilder from Virginia, and Deval Patrick of Massachusetts

title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
excerpt: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for i
body: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China

It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy
When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed

In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public
Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations
In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations
In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice

It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling
Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China
A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia

Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms
The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online
In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option
Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled
Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround

The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
url:
<title>From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771677/original/file-20261112-94-xxvbrd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8073%2C5382&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Jensen Huang: in the spotlight and out of a job.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/jensen-huang-speaks-on-stage-at-the-invest-in-germany-news-photo/2301028013?phrase=Jensen%20Huang&amp;adppopup=true">Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Extramarital activities have <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-affair.html">led to the resignation of</a> one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”</p>

<p>Huang stepped down following <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/technology/nvidia-investigation-jensen-huang-china.html">media reports</a> of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive <a href="https://thehill.com/policy/international/6212857-alice-huang-spy-allegations-nvidia-ceo-relationship/">suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies</a>. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/12/nvidia-megaspeed-alice-huang-jensen-.html">under U.S. scrutiny</a> for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.</p>

<p>Jensen Huang <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/a-message-to-our-company">acknowledged an affair</a>. And amid reports of a second <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-affair.html">with a company executive who reports to him</a>, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.</p>

<p>The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as <a href="https://www.belfercenter.org/publication/artificial-intelligence-and-national-security">central to national security</a> – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has <a href="https://x.com/CGTNEurope/status/2119783595040702490">denied the espionage allegations</a> and <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/12/china-says-us-fabricating-nvidia-spy-claims-to-justify-tech-blockade">accused the U.S.</a> of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/statement-from-nvidia-board-of-directors">it has no reason to believe</a> company secrets have been leaked.</p>

<p>Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is <a href="https://engelsbergideas.com/notebook/a-short-history-of-the-honey-trap/">history is dotted</a> with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.</p>

<p>Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “<a href="https://doi.org/10.17265/2159-5542/2025.05.001">beauty stratagem</a>.”</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=zh-CN&amp;user=SfkpAykAAAAJ">scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations</a>, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.</p>

<h2>The beauty stratagem of Ancient China</h2>

<p>“Meiren ji” is one of “<a href="https://www.amazon.com/dp/1533638780?lv=shuf&amp;channelId=500&amp;plpRedirect=mhFallback">Thirty-Six Stratagems</a>,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.  </p>

<p>The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.</p>

<p>Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/Spring-and-Autumn-Period">Spring and Autumn period</a> of Chinese history.</p>

<p>In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.  </p>

<p>According to the ancient historical text “<a href="https://cornellpress.cornell.edu/book/9781501754340/spring-and-autumn-annals-of-wu-and-yue/#bookTabs=1">Wu Yue Chun Qiu</a>,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.</p>

<p>The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An etching shows two women under Chinese writing." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771685/original/file-20261112-64-3g114.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A 19th-century etching depicting Zheng Dan and Xi Shi.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%E5%8F%A4%E4%BB%8A%E7%99%BE%E7%BE%8E%E5%9C%96%E4%B9%8B%E9%84%AD%E6%97%A6%E8%A5%BF%E6%96%BD%EF%BC%88One_hundred_beauties_Zheng_Dan_and_Xi_Shi%EF%BC%89.png">Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat <a href="https://www.chiculture.org.hk/sc/china-five-thousand-years/3946?utm_source=chatgpt.com">involved poor political decisions</a> and Yue’s military recovery.</p>

<p>Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.</p>

<p>A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “<a href="https://threekingdoms.com/">Romance of the Three Kingdoms</a>,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.</p>

<p>It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.</p>

<p>The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.</p>

<h2>The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware</h2>

<p>In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “<a href="https://thecsrjournal.in/honey-trapping-spy-tactic-threatening-national-security">honey trap</a>.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently <a href="https://foreignpolicy.com/2010/03/12/the-history-of-the-honey-trap/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">during the Cold War</a>.</p>

<p>Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the <a href="https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,1946375_1946448_1948269,00.html">Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu</a>. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>A more recent example involves <a href="https://abcnews4.com/news/nation-world/swalwell-and-fang-fang-declassified-fbi-files-reveal-physical-relationship-chinese-intelligence-congressional-office">former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang</a>, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.</p>

<h2>Why Jensen Huang is strategically important</h2>

<p>Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/insight-us-semiconductor-export-controls-update?utm_source=chatgpt.com">repeatedly tightened restrictions</a> on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.</p>

<p>Beijing is <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/china-sets-up-475-bln-state-fund-boost-semiconductor-industry-2024-05-27/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development</a>. Yet Chinese companies still <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/chinas-ai-chip-deficit-why-huawei-cant-catch-nvidia-and-us-export-controls-should-remain?utm_source=chatgpt.com">need advanced chips</a> to train AI models and build data centers.</p>

<p>From <a href="https://app.www.gov.cn/govdata/gov/201707/20/408540/article.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com">Beijing’s perspective</a>, advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition.</p>

<p>This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang.</p>

<p>However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation.</p>

<h2>Espionage in the age of AI</h2>

<p>Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages.</p>

<p>What has changed is who controls important strategic resources.</p>

<p>In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies.</p>

<p>More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently.</p>

<p>But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296393/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.” Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies
She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips
And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him , he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026
The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue

China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked
Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose

Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “ beauty stratagem .” As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations , I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today
As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors

The beauty stratagem of Ancient China “Meiren ji” is one of “ Thirty-Six Stratagems ,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE

Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership
The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience
Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history
In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit
But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge
According to the ancient historical text “ Wu Yue Chun Qiu ,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs
Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat
Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu
A 19th-century etching depicting Zheng Dan and Xi Shi
Wikimedia Commons Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear
Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery
Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly
A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “ Romance of the Three Kingdoms ,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature
It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty
To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander
He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo
The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him
Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor

The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “ honey trap .” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China
Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War
One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu
The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship
Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China
The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s

title: Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution

<title>Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution</title>
    <content type="html"><p>Typically, when people hear about nitrates, it involves <a href="https://extension.psu.edu/nitrates-in-drinking-water">runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities</a> that can fuel harmful algae blooms and raise the risk of a serious illness in infants known as “<a href="https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/water/blue-baby-syndrome.htm">blue baby syndrome</a>.”</p>

<p>But a river can also run through a sparsely populated landscape with little farming and still contain surprisingly high levels of this form of nitrogen that can harm aquatic life, drinking water and human health.</p>

<p>In a new study, my colleague and <a href="https://scholar.google.co.uk/citations?user=DJvp_4EAAAAJ&amp;hl=th">I</a> found a reason why that happens: Dry climate conditions are <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg2366">associated with high river nitrate concentrations</a>, even in places with little farming or urban development.</p>

<p>We found <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg2366">nitrate hot spots</a> in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains of the western United States and northern Africa’s Sahara Desert. Where water is scarce, we found that nitrates – which can naturally <a href="https://archive.cdc.gov/www_atsdr_cdc_gov/csem/nitrate-nitrite/where_are.html">leach into surface water and groundwater from the soil</a> as microbes break down organic material – were able to accumulate and become concentrated rather than being diluted or flushed away.</p>

<p>That raises health concerns for regions where nitrates in rivers and well water might not be given much thought. It also raises questions about how nitrate-related health risks will increase as global temperatures rise.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A maps shows high nitrate levels in the U.S., Europe and India, as well as across dry parts of Africa." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=276&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=276&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=276&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766628/original/file-20261015-50-wrknw9.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=347&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A global map of predicted river nitrate concentrations reveals elevated concentrations in arid, remote regions.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Li Li, et al., 2026</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>To see how widespread this pattern is, we combined global measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites and additionally extracted information about climate, soils, land use and other landscape features. We then trained machine learning models to <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg2366">estimate long-term average nitrate concentrations</a> across nearly 2.9 million river segments worldwide.</p>

<p>The resulting map suggests that nitrates deserve attention well beyond the urban and agricultural regions where they are usually monitored.</p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>High nitrate exposure in water and food is particularly dangerous for infants because it can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. <a href="https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/water/blue-baby-syndrome.htm">Blue baby syndrome</a>, or methemoglobinemia, can result in serious illnesses and be caused by nitrate poisoning.</p>

<p>The U.S. <a href="https://wqa.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/2014_NitrateNitrite.pdf">drinking water standard</a> of 10 milligrams of nitrate-nitrogen per liter was established primarily to guard against this acute risk.</p>

<p>We estimate that about 37,000 people worldwide live in areas where rivers exceed the 10 mg/L drinking water standard, predominantly in the U.S. Corn Belt.</p>

<p>That doesn’t mean 37,000 people are drinking water at those concentrations, since river water in many regions is treated before it is supplied for drinking. But it’s a concerning level they should be aware of, <a href="https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/environment/water/wells/waterquality/nitrate.html">particularly those using well water</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="3 women in a farmhouse kitchen" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771706/original/file-20261112-64-lwrk50.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Rural well water can carry more nitrates than residents realize.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/three-women-laughing-and-chatting-together-in-a-royalty-free-image/2282037692">Curly photo/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Research has also raised concerns about possible effects of long-term exposure to nitrate at lower concentrations, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.puhe.2024.01.001">including certain cancers</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeem.2025.103197">adverse birth outcomes</a>, such as babies born preterm or with a low birth weight, although those risks are still being studied. </p>

<p>We estimate that about 480 million people worldwide live in areas where nearby rivers have elevated long-term average nitrate concentrations, above 2.5 milligrams per liter.</p>

<p>Many of the rivers our models identified as having elevated nitrate levels are small headwater streams. Many headwater streams cease to flow for some periods of time every year, and nitrates can accumulate to high concentrations under dry or low-flow conditions. These small streams make up <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44221-025-00549-x">most of the global river networks</a>, have long been overlooked and feed larger rivers that supply drinking water to large populations and help shape the quality of water downstream.</p>

<p>Too much nitrate in rivers and lakes can also <a href="https://theconversation.com/toxic-algae-blooms-are-lasting-longer-in-lake-erie-why-thats-a-worry-for-people-and-pets-259954">fuel algal growth</a> and disrupt aquatic ecosystems. </p>

<h2>What we still don’t know</h2>

<p>A global map of nitrate concentrations in river water cannot show what comes out of someone’s tap. Their water may be mixed with other sources or <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/about/how-water-treatment-works.html">treated before they drink it</a>. Nitrate concentrations can also rise and fall over time, while our map shows long-term averages.</p>

<p>To understand a person’s actual exposure will require connecting river measurements with drinking water sources, treatment practices and tests of water delivered to households. </p>

<p>Many rivers with nitrate concentrations above 2.5 milligrams per liter flow through sparsely populated regions where access to treated drinking water may be limited. Even where treatment facilities exist, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-76040-2_26">conventional methods remove little nitrate</a>. Removing it requires <a href="https://extension.psu.edu/nitrates-in-drinking-water">specialized technologies</a> that can be costly to operate.</p>



<h2>What comes next</h2>

<p>Our study shows why more drylands and small headwater streams need to be monitored for nitrate. It also raises a question for a warming world: If a region becomes drier, how much will nitrate concentrations rise even if people do not add more nitrogen to the landscape?</p>

<p>Answering that will require measurements through wet and dry periods, paired with studies of how water moves through soils, groundwater and rivers. For now, the message is clear: Protecting water quality requires paying attention to the climate as well as to the human activities that put nitrogen into the environment.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294558/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><p>Mountains of scientific evidence <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2022.817808">support both the negative</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/ijamh-2023-0077">positive effects</a> of <a href="https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/f06e1673-3689-4cb1-8a37-762a3e9c5360/content">our eating habits on our health</a>. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21501-type-2-diabetes">Type 2 diabetes</a>, heart disease and <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/4314-hypertension-high-blood-pressure">high blood pressure</a>.</p>

<p>This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001182">to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions</a>. </p>

<p>Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1559827620915425">food is just as important</a> as medication for health and wellness.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=qRJi0c0AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">researchers</a> <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/natalie-minton-915001332">whose work</a> focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.</p>

<h2>Fighting food insecurity</h2>

<p>Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.</p>

<p>Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, <a href="https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/food-nutrition-assistance/food-security-in-the-us/key-statistics-graphics">lived in food-insecure households</a> – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.</p>

<p>Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to <a href="https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/food">roughly 673 million</a>. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.</p>
