<h2>Forward momentum</h2>

<p>Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/28/nx-s1-6018272/food-health-trump-wellness-maha-rfk-jr">Make American Healthy Again movement</a>, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has <a href="https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/6173378-rfk-jr-hospital-food-pledge/">brought new energy and attention</a> to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “<a href="https://realfood.gov/">Eat Real Food</a>.”</p>

<p>But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/28/health/h-jack-geiger-dead.html">Dr. Jack Geiger</a>. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.</p>

<p>When government officials <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001182">chastised him for prescribing food</a> to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”</p>

<p>Since then, thousands of community organizations like <a href="https://www.servings.org/">Community Servings</a> and <a href="https://www.openhand.org/">Project Open Hand</a> have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.</p>

<p>In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001182">review current food is medicine research</a> and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001182">saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually</a>.</p>

<p>Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the <a href="https://www.fimglobalalliance.org/about">Food Is Medicine Global Alliance</a>. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has <a href="https://www.fimglobalalliance.org/news-and-events">released several reports</a> highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.</p>

<h2>Food is medicine in our local community</h2>

<p>Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.</p>

<p>One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/2752535X241301847">statistically significant reductions in weight</a>, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.</p>

<p>For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with <a href="https://www.thehappyfoodsproject.org/">local farmers</a>. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers <a href="https://doi.org/10.5304/jafscd.2026.153.016">reported high satisfaction</a> with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.</p>

<h2>What other researchers have found</h2>

<p>One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001343">positively influenced diet quality and food security</a>.</p>

<p>Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcjd.2022.11.001">reductions in blood sugar levels</a>. This data supports our own previous findings.</p>

<p>However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/19320248.2024.2328344">supplemented only four to five meals each week</a>, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.</p>

<p>Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have <a href="https://www.iea.org/commentaries/energy-crisis-threatens-worlds-most-vulnerable-as-cooking-fuel-shortages-grow">increased prices of staple food products</a> like cereals and vegetable oil and led to <a href="https://www.fao.org/worldfoodsituation/FoodPricesIndex/en/">shortages of cooking oil</a> in some countries.</p>

<p>Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001343">adequately track clinical outcomes</a> from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293312/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too</title>
    <content type="html"><p>When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.</p>

<p>Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available.</p>

<p>As climate change increases the <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/extreme-weather/">frequency and intensity of extreme weather events</a> around the world, <a href="https://www.who.int/europe/emergencies/situations/climate-crisis-extreme-weather">these effects</a> can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit.</p>

<p>I study <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=47zNB8IAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">how political and environmental risks affect international business</a>. In my new book, “<a href="https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/management/international-business/multinational-corporations-and-climate-change-risks-responsibilities-and-resilience">Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience</a>,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether.</p>



<p>Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away.</p>

<h2>How climate risk affects foreign investment</h2>

<p>Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14693062.2023.2237479">systematically avoiding</a> investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/management/international-business/multinational-corporations-and-climate-change-risks-responsibilities-and-resilience">my own analysis</a> of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11625-022-01199-8">received less foreign investment</a>. </p>

<p>The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This <a href="https://gain.nd.edu/our-work/country-index/">vulnerability data</a> measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt.</p>

<p><iframe id="p8aCZ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/p8aCZ/4/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Scatter plot shows how investment is lower for climate-vulnerable countries"></iframe></p>

<p>Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible.</p>

<p>For example, <a href="https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/google-pauses-chilean-data-center-project-to-rethink-water-use/">Google halted plans</a> to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/8/24/can-kenyas-ai-ambitions-coexist-with-naivashas-water-needs">ultimately suspended</a> amid concerns about water stress in the area.</p>

<p>Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks.</p>

<p>One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a <a href="https://www.fm.com/insights/pentland-flood">5% average decline in shareholder value</a> over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements.</p>

<p>In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure <a href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099122424015054265/pdf/P178411-e9934965-b1ab-4306-a174-db4a84439d50.pdf">cost companies there about $280 million</a>.</p>

<p>Severe <a href="https://www.spglobal.com/content/dam/spglobal/s1/en/documents/general/S1-0826-Thailand-EEC-road-flooding-analysis-v2.pdf">flooding in Thailand</a> in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there.</p>

<p>Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next.</p>

<p>While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations.</p>

<h2>Who loses from investor avoidance?</h2>

<p>For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer <a href="https://www.emerald.com/ijdi/article-abstract/25/1-2/40/1301982/Navigating-the-labour-landscape-does-FDI-influence">jobs are created</a>. These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1057/9780230522954_3">new technologies that multinationals bring</a> when they invest abroad.</p>

<p>Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being.</p>

<p>Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-011-0346-8">their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure</a>. A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago <a href="https://climate.uchicago.edu/news/poor-countries-could-suffer-90-of-all-heat-related-deaths-by-2050/">projects that 90% of heat-related deaths</a> in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-30727-4">around 90% of people exposed to flooding</a> live in developing nations.</p>

<p><iframe id="HJVND" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/HJVND/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Countries' climate vulnerability worldwide shows most vulnerable are in Africa, South Asia and Oceania"></iframe></p>

<p>Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/9/4/how-much-does-africa-contribute-to-global-carbon-emissions">African countries</a> are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change.</p>

<h2>Lost opportunities for multinational companies</h2>

<p>When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company.</p>

<p>Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities.</p>

<p>For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo <a href="https://www.un.org/en/explainers/critical-minerals">supplies most of the world’s cobalt</a>, while Indonesia has become the <a href="https://www.igfmining.org/resource/nickel-mining-indonesia/">dominant producer of nickel</a>. <p>Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/news/freeport-grasberg-deal-reshapes-long-151119370.html">established strong</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.exis.2026.101934">positions in those countries’ mineral industries</a>. Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets.</p>

<h2>Reducing investor avoidance</h2>

<p>There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/17565529.2025.2471791">climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid</a> for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed.</p></li>
<li><p>International development banks can share some of the risks by providing <a href="https://www.swissre.com/risk-knowledge/mitigating-climate-risk.html">climate risk insurance</a> to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries <a href="https://www.miga.org/press-release/miga-supports-kenyas-geothermal-and-solar-power-growth">such as Kenya</a>, <a href="https://www.miga.org/press-release/miga-guarantee-helps-expand-clean-energy-access-remote-mozambique">Mozambique</a> and <a href="https://www.miga.org/press-release/miga-supports-private-renewable-energy-trading-platform-nigeria">Nigeria</a>.</p></li>
<li><p>Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many <a href="https://gain.nd.edu/">risk</a> <a href="https://www.germanwatch.org/en/cri">scores</a> label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295591/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Despite intense Islamophobia, Abdul El-Sayed and dozens of other Muslims elected representatives are breaking down barriers</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771160/original/file-20261110-64-5w7hs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6095%2C4063&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed walks in the halls of the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Congress/281fd4187ddb498792d68fb8217a68e7/photo">AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history on Nov. 3, 2026, when <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/abdul-el-sayed-becomes-first-muslim-elected-us-senate-2026-11-04/">Michigan voters elected him the first Muslim to the U.S. Senate</a> despite significant efforts to defeat him. </p>

<p>He wasn’t alone. A <a href="https://www.cair.com/press_releases/breaking-cair-cair-action-report-record-97-muslims-and-counting-elected-nationwide/">record number of American Muslims won their races</a> in the midterms. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.nazitalajevardi.com/">political</a> <a href="https://www.su.se/english/profiles/k/krve3535">scientists</a> <a href="https://www.uu.se/en/contact-and-organisation/staff?query=N2-888">who study</a> minority politics, we think their wins raise a question that goes beyond any single race: What does it mean for Muslim Americans, and for everyone else, to see Muslims elected to public office? </p>

<h2>A tough campaign</h2>

<p>The August 2026 Democratic primary alone drew record-breaking outside spending from the <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/2/how-much-has-aipac-spent-against-michigans-abdul-el-sayed-and-why">pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC</a> and corporate special interests, totaling nearly US$70 million to defeat El-Sayed. That is about 11 times his own spending.</p>

<p>In the November 2026 midterm election, outside groups, including super PACs and other organizations independent of the campaigns, spent more than $134 million, according to <a href="https://votelog.org/investigations/michigan-senate-general-money">independent trackers</a>. The largest spender was the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC <a href="https://bridgemi.com/michigan-politics/mike-rogers-vs-abdul-el-sayed-what-to-know-about-us-senate-race-in-michigan/">aligned with some Senate Republican leaders</a>.</p>

<p>El-Sayed also broke with his party’s leadership on Gaza. As a candidate, he called for <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/04/nx-s1-6028702/abdul-el-sayed-michigan-senate-israel-aid">ending U.S. arms sales to Israel</a> and opposed what he called “<a href="https://www.metrotimes.com/news/politics-elections/el-sayed-defies-democratic-partys-establishment-on-gaza-in-senate-race/">blank-check military aid</a>” to any foreign country. That stance resonated with the many Arab and Muslim Americans who had <a href="https://bridgemi.com/michigan-politics/how-despair-over-gaza-war-helped-donald-trump-win-dearborn-its-complicated/">split with Democrats</a> over the war in 2024. </p>

<p>El-Sayed also faced a barrage of openly Islamophobic attacks expressing hatred or hostility toward Islam or Muslims. President Donald Trump called him a “<a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/25/trump-escalates-campaign-rhetoric-calling-el-sayed-jihadist/">jihadist</a>” and a “Muslim Brotherhood guy.” Vice President <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/01/abdul-el-sayed-jd-vance-evil">JD Vance</a> accused him of supporting <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-sharia-law-and-why-is-it-so-controversial-in-the-united-states-294224">Sharia law</a>. And in the week after El-Sayed’s primary win, anti-Muslim posts targeting him online <a href="https://www.csohate.org/2026/08/12/abdul-el-sayed-islamophobia/">rose about twentyfold</a>.</p>

<p>El-Sayed won anyway. Across the country, at least <a href="https://www.cair.com/press_releases/breaking-cair-cair-action-report-record-97-muslims-and-counting-elected-nationwide/">97 American Muslims</a> won federal, state and local races this year, according to the Council on American-Islamic Relations. </p>

<h2>Why representation matters</h2>

<p>Political scientists have long studied descriptive representation – the election of politicians who share the background of the people they serve, such as their race, ethnicity, gender or religion. </p>

<p>One of the earliest studies came from sociologist <a href="https://bobo.scholars.harvard.edu/">Lawrence Bobo</a> and political scientist <a href="https://www.uncg.edu/employees/franklin-gilliam/">Franklin Gilliam Jr.</a>, who found that Black Americans living in cities with a Black mayor <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/1963525">were more politically engaged</a> than Black Americans elsewhere. Those who resided in cities with a Black mayor were more likely to report being trusting of government, more confident that they could make a difference and more attentive to politics. </p>

<p>Later scholars called this the “minority empowerment thesis,” meaning that when members of a minority group are elected, other members of that group feel more connected to politics. For example, political scientists <a href="https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/staff/profiles/gov/banducci-susan">Susan A. Banducci</a>, <a href="https://chss.wwu.edu/political-science/people/todd-donovan">Todd Donovan</a> and <a href="https://www.brunel.ac.uk/people/jeffrey-karp">Jeffrey A. Karp</a> found that Black Americans represented by a Black member of Congress were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2508.2004.00163.x">significantly more likely</a> than other Black Americans to know their representative’s name. They were also more likely to have contacted their representative and to remember something they had done for the district.</p>

<h2>Exclusion can push Muslims out of public life</h2>

<p>For Muslim Americans, the stakes are especially high because research shows that, at times, hostility pushes them away from public life. </p>

<p>During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump called for “<a href="https://www.npr.org/2015/12/07/458836388/trump-calls-for-total-and-complete-shutdown-of-muslims-entering-u-s">a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States</a>.” Around that time, users of the social media platform X, then known as Twitter, who had Arabic names shared their locations <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055418000801">10% to 20% less often</a>. It was a sign that they were making themselves less visible online. In the same study, Muslim Americans surveyed in early 2017 who reported experiencing societal discrimination also indicated avoiding public places – such as restaurants, shopping malls and parks – and limiting what they posted online. </p>

<p>Political scientist <a href="https://polisci.msu.edu/people/directory/sediqe-nura.html">Nura Sediqe</a> has studied what social psychologist <a href="https://www.uvm.edu/cas/psychology/profile/elizabeth-pinel">Elizabeth Pinel</a> called “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S104909652000075X">stigma consciousness</a>”: expecting to be judged and treated differently because of a part of one’s identity that others look down on. In a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S104909652000075X">survey of Muslims</a> in southeast Michigan, Sediqe found that the more strongly they expected this, the less likely they were to identify as American. That expectation was highest among those who had faced discrimination and among women who wear the hijab, a headscarf that is a visible marker of their faith. In other words, being made to feel like an outsider can weaken Muslims’ sense that they belong in the country, and in its democracy.</p>

<p>Muslims also face barriers from elected officials of both parties. In an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/21565503.2018.1528161">audit study</a> of state legislators in all 50 states, for example, both Democrats and Republicans were less likely to respond to a Muslim constituent than a white one.</p>

<h2>What our research finds</h2>

<p>To understand what visible Muslim representation can change, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.electstud.2023.102741">we conducted two experiments</a> in May 2022. We created a one-minute animated video showing “a day in the life of a city council member,” designed to resemble the short explainer videos that companies and government agencies use online to explain their work to the public.</p>

<p>Survey respondents were randomly assigned to watch one of two versions. In one, three council members were visibly Muslim. In the other, the same three characters appeared without religious symbols. Because the videos were otherwise identical, any differences in how people responded can be attributed to seeing Muslims on the council. The first study surveyed 740 American Muslims, and the second nearly 4,000 non-Muslim Americans.</p>

<p>In both studies, people who saw the council with visibly Muslim members judged it to be fairer and more legitimate. The effect was strongest among Muslims, but non-Muslims rated the council slightly fairer and more legitimate, too.</p>

<p>Muslim participants who saw visibly Muslim leaders were also more willing to take part in politics. On average, they were about 5 percentage points more likely to say they planned to do things like contact a public official, attend a local political meeting or join a protest in the coming year. They also showed a small increase in interest in running for office.</p>

<h2>Representation is not zero-sum</h2>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman wearing a star-patterned headdress, surrounded by a crowd of people raising their fists and holding signs." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771161/original/file-20261110-64-pyp7nz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Research suggests that seeing Muslim leaders can make Muslim Americans more willing to take part in politics.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election%202026%20First%20Muslim%20Senator/7b4aba8bc35b4a8d97bb86f17da1e939/photo">AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our research suggests that representation is not zero-sum, meaning that making a political body more inclusive for one group did not come at the expense of another. That challenges a common worry that elevating one group will alienate everyone else. Readers should note that we used short animated videos of a fictional city council, not real elected officials, so more research is needed to know how these effects play out with real politicians and how long they last. </p>

<p>Still, these findings do matter in a moment like this one. During the campaign, <a href="https://www.ms.now/rachel-maddow-show/maddowblog/nancy-mace-muslim-islam-hate-bigotry-republican-party-gop-el-sayed">Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina posted</a> that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse and a threat to both national security and our republic.” </p>

<p>But our research points the other way. Seeing Muslims in office made both Muslims and non-Muslims alike view a political body as fairer and more legitimate. </p>

<p>We argue that El-Sayed’s presence in the Senate, alongside the record number of Muslims elected across the country, has the potential to not only show Muslim Americans that they belong in American democracy, but also to show everyone else that the country’s institutions are stronger for it.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296035/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Rural women in Colorado and nationwide are at higher risk for cervical cancer – at-home test kits can help close the gap</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767108/original/file-20261019-50-mmby8p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8192%2C5461&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Women now have more options for cervical cancer screening.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/female-doctor-talking-with-young-woman-in-exam-room-royalty-free-image/2164283046">MoMo Productions/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>With vaccines and regular screening, cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers.</p>

<p>Yet women living in rural areas of the United States have a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.62634">25% higher rate of cervical cancer</a> – and a 42% higher rate of death from the disease compared to urban women.  </p>

<p>In Colorado, rural counties such as Prowers, Moffat and Montrose have almost <a href="https://cohealthviz.dphe.state.co.us/t/HealthInformaticsPublic/views/COHID2020-2022CancerIncidenceRates/AgeAdjustedRatesDashboard?%3Aembed=y&amp;%3AisGuestRedirectFromVizportal=y">three times the rate of cervical cancer than urban counties</a>.</p>

<p>Nationwide, 13,000 women are diagnosed with the disease and more than <a href="https://gis.cdc.gov/Cancer/USCS/#/">4,000 die from it each year</a>. In Colorado, the most recent data available indicated that almost <a href="https://cohealthviz.dphe.state.co.us/t/HealthInformaticsPublic/views/CCCR2000-2022CancerIncidenceRates-CoHID/CountsDashboard?%3Aembed=y&amp;%3AisGuestRedirectFromVizportal=y">150 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2023</a>, and, on average, <a href="https://cohealthviz.dphe.state.co.us/t/HealthInformaticsPublic/views/COHIDDeathsDashboardAllYearsExcludesRace/DeathDashboardAllYearsexcludesrace">more than 40 women die annually</a>. </p>

<p>While <a href="https://gis.cdc.gov/Cancer/USCS/#/">overall numbers of diagnoses and deaths nationwide have decreased</a> over the past 20 years, rural women are more likely to be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.62634">diagnosed at a later stage of disease</a>, meaning chemotherapy and radiation treatments may be necessary to treat their disease.</p>

<p><a href="https://som.cuanschutz.edu/Profiles/Faculty/Profile/19930">My research and clinical expertise</a> in gynecology and obstetrics specifically aim to tackle this troubling health disparity. I study lower genital tract precancers from human papillomavirus, or HPV. As part of a team of researchers across the U.S., I <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.11081">participated in a clinical trial</a> that led to the first FDA-approved at-home HPV test. </p>

<p>The development of an at-home test is a game changer. It can bring screening to a broader spectrum of women, hopefully catching those who have precancerous changes early enough to prevent the progression to cancer. </p>

<p>But eliminating cervical cancer will require ensuring that women can access not only screening but also vaccines and any necessary follow-up diagnostic procedures and treatments. </p>

<h2>A simple swab test at home</h2>

<p>For rural women, access to healthcare clinics for routine screenings may be limited. A visit to a qualified professional for a cervical exam and Pap test can require half a day or longer in travel and wait times. In a recent study, women in rural counties were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/jrh.70210">20% less likely to be up to date on cervical cancer screening</a>. </p>

<p>In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized the <a href="https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpmn/denovo.cfm?id=DEN240045">Teal Wand for at-home self-collection</a>.  Federal and medical organizations have since included self-collection as part of routine screening recommendations. My university received funding from Teal Health to support research. I was a site investigator, but I have no shares in the company or any patents, and I have never received any money directly from Teal. </p>

<p>Women can now also do a test during a visit to their primary care doctor even if that doctor does not perform pelvic exams. That means patients do not need to see a gynecologist to get screened. </p>

<p>Nearly all cervical cancers are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2023.13174">caused by persistent viral infections</a> from HPV. These infections most frequently occur through sexual contact. At-home screening tests check for infection, which means clinicians can identify women at risk of developing cervical cancer before the disease occurs. </p>

<p>During self-collection, women use a simple swab to collect a vaginal sample. That swab is mailed to the lab and then tested for HPV. </p>

<p>Studies have shown that when FDA-approved HPV tests are used, self-collected samples are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.11081">as reliable as clinician-collected samples</a> for detecting cervical precancer.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Vaginal fluid sample in a white plastic container with a white cap for cervical cancer screening." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=607&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=607&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=607&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=763&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=763&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767111/original/file-20261019-50-lpm2jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=763&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Screening early for cervical cancer can help find precancer disease.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/vaginal-fluid-sample-for-cervical-cancer-screening-royalty-free-image/1849234816">Md Babul Hosen/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Closing the access gap</h2>

<p>Studies show that self-collection tests for HPV can help decrease barriers to care for rural communities. A study across four Appalachian state regions – Ohio, West Virginia, Kentucky and Virginia – found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-24-099">screening increases when women are mailed a self-collection kit</a>. Appalachia, a largely rural geographic region that is underserved in terms of access to healthcare, has documented disparities in cervical cancer rates. </p>

<p>Underscreened patients across these four states were randomly chosen to either receive the usual care, a mailed reminder letter to go to a clinic or a mailed HPV self-collection kit. The study showed a threefold increase in screening rates: 5% with the reminder and 15% with the mailed kits. </p>

<p>Another study in Washington state showed similar results, with an increase in screening of overdue individuals by more than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2023.21471">15% in mailed kits versus education alone</a>.</p>

<p>Statewide initiatives in Alabama, with the <a href="https://operationwipeout.org/">Operation Wipe Out project</a>, and in Texas, with the <a href="https://www.texascancerplan.org/ccep/">Lone Star Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan</a>, use self-screening as part of a strategy to eliminate cervical cancer. </p>

<p>In Colorado, I am part of a team working to implement a similar plan that we hope to initiate in 2027.</p>

<p>Studies in Europe <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14796694.2024.2409625">have shown that self-collection</a> has increased access to care, improved screening rates and reduced screening costs. Long-term evidence demonstrates these programs are effective: Many countries began using them as early as 2017.</p>

<p>Making screening easier is only the first step toward preventing cervical cancer. Even in the Appalachian study, fewer than 15 out of 100 women who <a href="https://doi.org/10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-24-0999">received mailed HPV self-collection kits completed screening</a>.</p>

<p>In short, removing the need for a clinic visit does not address all the barriers to preventing this disease. </p>

<h2>Screening combined with vaccines and mobile clinics</h2>

<p>HPV vaccines are the single strongest tool <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30068-4">for preventing cervical cancer</a>. Vaccinations are recommended for adolescents ages 9-14 before they are exposed to HPV. If given under age 15, two shots six months apart are required. No booster is needed. Individuals who do not receive the vaccine before turning 15 can get a “catch-up” vaccine as a three-shot series up to age 45. </p>

<p>For women who test positive for high-risk HPV, additional testing may be necessary to identify precancerous changes in the cervix. In rural communities, accessing these services can be even more challenging than obtaining screening.</p>

<p>Mobile clinics can bring services closer to patients. Training more clinicians to provide colposcopy services could improve access to diagnostic care. <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/colposcopy/about/pac-20385036">Colposcopy is an exam</a> in which a healthcare provider uses a lighted magnifying instrument to look closely at the cervix for abnormal or precancerous changes. A small tissue sample may be taken for diagnostic testing.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2025.2971">Patient navigators and community health workers</a> can also assist women in overcoming barriers to care. A patient navigator is a trained professional who helps overcome roadblocks by providing education, coordinating services, connecting patients with resources and supporting them through the healthcare system to ensure timely access to care.</p>

<p>Rural women in Colorado and elsewhere urgently need a concerted effort from statewide programs and health centers to decrease the incidence and deaths from this disease. </p>

<p>No one should die from cervical cancer.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293083/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
