title: Jensen Huang is out. What now?
excerpt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in October 2026. | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images The first big sex scandal of the AI era has taken down Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s co-fou
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in October 2026. | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images The first big sex scandal of the AI era has taken down Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO
Nvidia’s board of directors announced his resignation on Thursday morning and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO

Huang has been making headlines all week after news broke Friday that he had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singaporean tech firm Megaspeed who the US government alleges was also a Chinese spy

The revelation Wednesday of a second extramarital affair , this time with an Nvidia employee reporting to Huang directly, added to the pressure, and another affair came to light later on Thursday after Huang’s ouster
The scandal has implications far beyond one company: Huang’s central role in the AI race can’t be overstated

It was his vision of an AI future that led him to pivot Nvidia from a small company making video game chips into the dominant player in making the chips that serve OpenAI , Anthropic, and Google’s computing needs
Huang is close friends with President Donald Trump’s and a leading voice in resisting efforts to slow AI progress
And he has pushed for the US to take a less hawkish position toward China’s own AI goals , a stance now called into question by his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy
Among its other impacts, the news has revived efforts on Capitol Hill to further restrict chip exports to China

To break down the national security implications of Huang’s departure, how the Trump administration is involved, and what it says about US AI industry writ large, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Garret De Vynck , a technology reporter at the Washington Post
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Nvidia has been called the central bank of AI, which is why it’s so important that we figure out what Jensen Huang may have disclosed to this alleged spy

How long has the president known about this, as far as we know? As far as we know, the president has known about the fact that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with someone that the US government thought was a spy for about a year
This circulated within the administration, and the decision was made not to tell Jensen
That doesn’t necessarily mean that it was automatically some kind of corrupt decision of President Trump protecting Jensen Huang
There’s all sorts of reasons why you might not want to tell someone they’re being spied on, the number one being that they might blow up the operation
Maybe you suspect that the person themselves knows that they’re being spied on and is willingly sharing information and you need some more time to gather that

It’s unclear why the US government specifically chose not to pull in Jensen Huang.  It’s also a little bit unclear whether he knows he was being spied on, or whether maybe he was told through some kind of back channel
He has said that he did not know that she was a spy and he is admitting to the affair, to the infidelity

He’s admitting to essentially breaking Nvidia’s code of conduct by sleeping with one of its customers, but he is not admitting at all to knowing that she was a spy and definitely not admitting to sharing any information willfully
It feels like this is the kind of thing that the government would investigate
There’s been reporting that the Commerce Department was involved with some kind of investigation, but that investigation came to an end and no one really knows why
The context here is that the United States and China are in an AI race

Going back to the first Trump administration, there’s been pretty aggressive export controls saying, “We don’t want China to get our tech so that they can develop AI.” And the Biden administration continued that
He increased the export controls on China
China was complaining very loudly about this
We want to win AI and we need to slow you guys down.’ When Trump came in, he actually lifted his foot off the gas a little bit
They didn’t throw the gates open and say, “You can have whatever you want
All American companies can sell whatever they want to China.” But he said, “Some AI chips that are less powerful than the state of the art

We can send those to Chinese companies.“ The other thing that national security experts have pointed out is that the Trump administration could theoretically have been doing more to stop the smuggling of computer chips to China
And that’s where this story gets so important for national security
Megaspeed is accused of essentially being a front for Chinese companies to get access to computer chips
Journalists have gone to Megaspeed’s office in Singapore where it’s based, and there were only a couple of people working there
It didn’t really seem like there was a lot going on

Nvidia has said all through this process over the last couple of years that, “No, we’ve checked it out, Megaspeed is a legitimate company and we’re not breaking the law when it comes to this.” There are a lot of questions and what everyone is focused on finding out, both journalists and I would say congressional Democrats when they come into office in the new year is, is there something more going on here? Is there something where the Chinese either convinced Jensen Huang to sell more chips to them or Jensen Huang himself, who has been advocating for selling more chips to China, essentially did this himself?  “I think there’s this real question of: Do we see a much stronger push to actually ramp up controls on China and how does Trump respond?” He’s been pressuring the president, he’s been donating to him , he’s been glad-handing with the president and the president has been listening more to this corporate executive who is his friend and who donated him a bunch of money rather than listening to China hawks or national security experts who say we should be limiting what China is able to access
That’s really where the locus of this investigation is going to be
It’s not so much that Jensen Huang had an affair

It’s more the fact that he himself is someone who has said we need to sell more computer chips to China and he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy, and he’s very close to the president and had influence on the president
Have they said anything? Are they going to call him in front of Congress for an investigation? Going forward, there are two big things here

title: Is this the end of the Electoral College?
excerpt: Boxes containing the Electoral College votes are carried into the House Chamber during a joint session of Congress to ratify the 2024 presidential election. | A
body: Boxes containing the Electoral College votes are carried into the House Chamber during a joint session of Congress to ratify the 2024 presidential election. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

I don’t know how much time you spend in the more feverish right-wing corners of the internet, but some conservative commentators are growing very alarmed about a specific Democratic policy proposal that could be nearing fruition
It’s not even investigating President Donald Trump over his reported failure to act on intelligence about his newly jobless/disgraced pal , Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang

Instead, they’re concerned about a wonky electoral workaround called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact , which would essentially sidestep the Electoral College. (And in the words of one right-wing commentator, “effectively [rig] the system so Democrats could never lose again.”)  NPV isn’t quite as nefarious as that (Trump won the popular vote just two years ago!), though it would revolutionize how the United States conducts presidential elections
The compact is basically an agreement between states to award their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how their own state voted
Once enough states sign on, their combined electoral votes would guarantee the presidency to whoever wins the national popular vote
The compact has laid dormant for two decades, however, while its backers lobby to sign on more states and their electoral votes

Eighteen states and Washington, DC, have signed on thus far, representing 222 votes.  But with Democrats soon controlling state governments in Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, NPV could finally gain the critical mass to become reality
Politico reported on Tuesday that lawmakers in several states, including Pennsylvania, are already discussing the possibility
There’s just one problem: Conservative influencers aren’t the only ones worried about the plan
In fact, even one of its architects has come to regard NPV as a “doomsday machine” that could trigger gigantic constitutional problems
Go a little deeper View Link My colleague Andrew Prokop called up this conflicted architect, the Yale University professor Akhil Amar , earlier this week
Andrew has been writing and thinking about NPV for years
But Amar has been thinking about it even longer — since the aftermath of the 2000 election that made George W
Bush president.  Famously, Bush was elected even though he lost the popular vote, which Al Gore won by roughly half a percentage point

Amar thought the Electoral College was historically and inherently flawed, but only a constitutional amendment could abolish it.  Recognizing the long odds there, Amar and his brother instead sketched out a quick thought experiment — the broad strokes of what is now the NPV compact
The concept was later picked up and championed by the computer scientist John Koza and his group National Popular Vote Inc
Koza has had quite a lot of success getting states to sign on to this workaround
But all the signees so far have leaned Democratic, which concerns Amar

The institution of the Electoral College doesn’t inherently favor one party over the other (in fact, both parties nearly got rid of it after the 1968 election), and the NPV wasn’t designed to tilt the scales, either

But as the discourse on right-wing social media suggests, Trump’s 2016 victory with a popular vote minority has only further hardened views on each side, and all the Democratic signatories have made it look like a partisan proposition.  There’s another problem too, Amar says
The compact leaves each participating state to calculate the national total, without a centralized body to oversee a nationwide count or recount
A very close election could leave states disagreeing over who won

But in the current environment, it’s actually hard to imagine a centralized body that both parties would find credible: People just don’t trust institutions the way they did in, say, 2000.  That puts NPV advocates in a tricky spot: The political process may finally favor the compact, but it faces significant cultural problems that could undermine its legitimacy.  Amar, for his part, thinks that even the small risk of electoral disruption outweighs the benefits of NPV

Especially since the Electoral College does actually work, whatever its shortcomings.  “The one thing we really do need to avoid as the stabilizing superpower in the world is constitutional chaos,” he told Vox. “And because this is sort of a new plan, even if it’s in principle likely to be better in all sorts of scenarios, if in a certain small percentage of cases it would lead to chaos, that’s something we need [to] seriously consider.” One link for later ➨ Stop subway scrolling

If social media feels exhausting and overwhelming to you — which it does to me, often — try to stop logging on from public places . “People feel more lonely when they use social media while in transit, around people they have close relationships with, and when they are in nature,” says Vox contributor Shayla Love. “In contrast, when people use social media for shorter periods when they are alone at home or in study locations, it doesn’t have as much of a negative effect.” Before you go… Did you know… that the invention of fabrics like Spandex and Lycra changed not only what we wear — but when and how we wear it? With the advent of stretchy fabrics, Parisian fashion houses and the silhouettes they designed lost some of their influence .  Today’s trivia: What type of nymphs live in trees, as opposed to water, caves or clouds? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you what type of music Leontyne Price performed
That would be opera: Price, now 99, was among the first Black American opera singers to achieve acclaim around the world.

title: How the 7 healthcare workers who just got elected to Congress plan to fix our broken system
excerpt: Newly elected members of Congress on Capitol Hill. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Last week’s blue tsunami carried a lot of white coats: At least seven newly elec
body: Newly elected members of Congress on Capitol Hill. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Last week’s blue tsunami carried a lot of white coats: At least seven newly elected Democrats have medical degrees or nursing careers

Pediatrician Annie Andrews of South Carolina scored one of the most shocking Senate victories of election night for Democrats, while Abdul El-Sayed (who earned a medical degree before working in public health) won the all-important Michigan Senate race

In the House, Democrats will soon welcome pediatrician Richard Pan of California , emergency room physician Amish Shah of Arizona , surgeon Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, emergency nurse Mitchell Berman of Wisconsin, and oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker of Ohio

Like many Democrats, these candidates campaigned on lowering costs, expanding health coverage, and confronting the drugmakers and healthcare corporations that they accuse of putting profits ahead of patients
They have endorsed big ideas to make healthcare better, from a public insurance option to Medicare-for-all, alongside targeted changes to drug prices and health insurance denials
With President Donald Trump still in the White House, Democrats’ healthcare agenda faces obvious obstacles in the short term

But I spoke with Pan and Shah this week to learn how they hope to influence the healthcare conversation in Washington going forward.  They may be politicians, but they have seen America’s broken healthcare up close

They’re hoping to help some of their new colleagues, who may not have those same experiences and may be prone to thinking of policy issues in abstract terms, understand the urgency and the human toll of our messed-up medical system

And as lawmakers try to come up with solutions to fix those problems, they’ll be there to make sure those policies actually make sense in practice. “For us, these policy discussions are not abstract,” Pan said. “As a practicing physician, I know what it’s like to be on the front lines and have to look a patient in the eye and even tell them that, well, these programs either exist or don’t exist, and we’re not going to be able to get you help

And those are the types of things I have to deal with each time I see a patient.” What practicing medicine teaches you about politics The new members will join a small but notable group of providers-turned-politicians: The Congressional Doctors Caucus, founded last year, had six Democratic members before last week’s midterms

Shah, who previously served in the Arizona legislature, told me that he believed his medical career had given him a valuable outlook for thinking about how to serve in political office. “The core function of practicing medicine is to care for people,” Shah said. “The same should really be true about politics.” He’s experienced the shocking inequities of US healthcare, and seen its impact on people’s well-being, firsthand
Earlier this year, Shah said, an uninsured woman came into his emergency room department with an allergic reaction
But she was worried about the bill, asking if she might have to pay a $10,000 charge after she was discharged
And Shah told me that he had to be honest with her that she might
That’s when he learned that his patient was her family’s breadwinner — and that she actually worked in a nearby emergency department

Somebody who helped provide emergency care to others couldn’t afford it herself. “It’s a tragedy that those of us who actually go out to help others and be part of the team that saves lives can be left without insurance,” Shah said
Pan, a former California state senator, described a similar experience while treating kids in primary care
He has seen all the ways US health care is lacking: children who don’t get the mental health support they need to excel in school, families that struggle to afford stable housing or find healthy food
His ability to help depended on decisions made well outside his examination room
Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems

How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy

Sign up here . “These are all things that certainly have potential policy solutions, but it’s not just theoretical,” he told me. “It is very real and tied to very specific patients that I’ve seen.” But while these experiences have made them eager to change things, the newly elected physicians are also mindful about how proposed changes could disrupt ongoing patient care

Pan said he wants to push his colleagues about both the intended and unintended consequences or new policies: Who will get help? What happens to people whose needs don’t fit neatly into boxes? As any doctor will tell you, every patient is unique
That’s especially true for people with chronic conditions, he said, who may have spent years finding the right doctors and treatments
Lawmakers have to strike a balance: identifying ideas that will improve the health system in the long term, without jeopardizing the care that people need right now
Shah said he hopes his experience as a physician can help Congress find a middle ground between the patients demanding reform and the providers who are wary of big changes

After decades in medicine and a stint in the state legislature, he knows the different players and their concerns. “I speak the language of healthcare,” he said. “I’ve earned the trust of a lot of those stakeholders that I will not take an axe to the system, but rather reform it in a way that really improves it and centers the patient

So that gives me a unique ability to improve this at the congressional level.” What the new doctors and nurses want to change These Democratic doctors, like their party’s leaders, have a clear No. 1 priority when they take office next year: reversing the $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts that Republicans passed as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025. “Given all the damage the Republicans did in the past two years, first we got to triage to stop the bleeding,” Pan told me
He wants to repeal the OBBBA’s Medicaid work requirements, restore the lapsed Affordable Care Act tax credits that helped reduce premiums for millions of Americans, and protect Medicare payments

Those were common themes across these physician-politicians: Andrews , Berman , and El-Sayed endorsed the same policies as part of their campaign platform, while Knickerbocker likewise pledged to protect Medicaid, Medicare, the ACA, and children’s health coverage

Beyond reversing the Republican cuts, the newcomers want to cover more people, though they have different ideas about how to do it. “You have these real stories that then drive the legislation, and give you the ideas to solve the problems for people.” Amish Shah, emergency room physician elected in Arizona Shah said he supports letting people buy into Medicare
Andrews, Berman, Knickerbocker, and Shah have also endorsed a public option: a government-backed health insurance plan that would compete with private plans

El-Sayed and Hamawy , meanwhile, say they favor Medicare-for-all, guaranteeing comprehensive coverage without premiums or out-of-pocket costs. “I want to see every United States citizen covered, and I’d like to see the premiums drop,” Shah said
But even the people who have health insurance often struggle to pay for medical care
Andrews, Berman, El-Sayed, and Hamawy have all proposed expanding the government’s negotiation of prescription drug prices
Andrews and Berman want to extend Medicare’s $35 insulin cap to private insurance
Andrews, Berman, and Hamawy also want to crack down on private equity ownership and consolidation among healthcare providers
Perhaps unsurprisingly, these doctors were not afraid to get into the weeds of healthcare policy on the campaign trail
Andrews’s detailed plans include limits on some hospital prices and changing Medicare payments so the same service costs the same regardless of where it is performed

Berman’s agenda draws on his own nursing experience: He wants nurses to help set staffing standards, more funding for nursing education, and enhance workplace safety for medical workers, a goal he shares with Shah

title: How science informs author Emily St. John Mandel’s fiction
excerpt: John Mandel in September 2016. | Ulf Andersen/Getty Images The world is full of unanswered questions and strange ideas
body: John Mandel in September 2016. | Ulf Andersen/Getty Images The world is full of unanswered questions and strange ideas

Do parallel universes exist? What would it look like if a pandemic wiped out life as we know it? Is time travel possible?  I host the science podcast Unexplainable , where we often speak to scientists about their attempts to puzzle through life’s greatest mysteries, but academic researchers aren’t the only people wrestling with these concepts
On the latest episode of the show, I spoke with Emily St
John Mandel, the award-winning author of Station Eleven , about her new book, Exit Party , which grapples with the question of the multiverse

We talked about how she approaches science in her fiction, and how, even if we never get clear answers to some of these strange ideas, they can still help us think deeply about ourselves and our world.  Below is an excerpt from our conversation, edited for clarity and length
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts and Spotify , or watch us on Netflix
Emily, you are often writing about really interesting scientific ideas
Why do you put these scientific concepts at the heart of the books that you write? Because they’re so interesting
I don’t have an educational background in science
I did work in a cancer research lab for years, so I’ve definitely hung out with scientists
But I could not actually tell you the mechanisms by which microRNA 335 impacts breast cancer metastasis, Neither can I
But you know what? Science is interesting to me
I like reading about ideas in the fringes of science
But my understanding is that physicists are more or less evenly split on the question of whether we’re living in a multiverse
Where do you start with exploring these concepts? It’s really book by book
Sea of Tranquility was the first book I wrote that had more of a hard sci-fi component, because I do have a time-traveling detective in that book
And what that came out of was it was the spring of 2020
I was promoting The Glass Hotel on Zoom, and I thought that for my own sanity, it might be nice to be immersed in the grand project of a book
That can be good for you sometimes when everything is chaos, like in the early days of a pandemic.  I’ve always loved time travel novels as a reader and a fan
The problem with the time travel narrative, though, is that it falls apart instantly

What do you mean?  If you think about it for a second, it’s like, if I walk out of this podcast studio and I’m transported back to 1812, was I not always going to walk out of the studio and be transported back to 1812? And doesn’t reality break upon my arrival? That raises other questions like immortality — am I always going round and round in time? The causation gets really complicated and weird
But I felt like, you know what? I’m going to write whatever I want
So I start writing about my time-traveling detective, and then I run into the time travel narrative problem, the loops and the paradoxes and all the rest of it

And my solve for that, I thought, “What if I added a whole other layer of science fictional weirdness to try to make that work?” Enter the simulation hypothesis, which is the hypothesis that all of our reality is a simulation
And something I love about that is you can find really smart people convincingly arguing either side
I thought it was a cool idea, and I realized that I could use that to make time travel work
And so that’s what got me into that little branch of science for Sea of Tranquility .  And then Exit Party , I had an idea about writing about doppelgängers
I’d been thinking about it for years — the idea of a counter life
Counter life? The life you did not live, where you moved to a different city or took a different job or married a different person — any of those inflection points
I wondered if doppelgängers could be thought of as a sort of embodiment of a counter life
It’s another you who has lived a different life in a different version of reality
That’s what got me to the multiverse idea
But then I was also thinking, “Okay, well, I’ve thought about the counter life of the individual
What is the counter life of the state?” And that can be a really interesting thought experiment
There are some very obvious inflection points in our recent history, but every country has them
You know, the election that went a different way or the decision made to go to war or not
A policy that was enacted or not enacted and the fallout from that, and any of those inflection points create a somewhat different country
It was thinking about counter lives and doubling, and that’s what got me to this idea of the multiverse
You’re talking about these ideas almost like, “It’s a fix to this problem that I created.”  It often is
Exit Party opens with a woman going to a party, two doppelgängers show up, and somebody else disappears

title: The disturbing reality behind America’s milk and cheese — and the fight to end it
excerpt: This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare
body: This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare
Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country
But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system

And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it.  At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies
Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation
Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them

Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef.  But whatever their ultimate market destination, the overwhelming majority of baby cows born in the dairy industry, in California and nationwide, spend their first few months of life housed alone, in individual crates or enclosures

Many of them look like this:  largest calf raiser in California . | Courtesy of Direct Action Everywhere (DxE)" data-portal-copyright="Courtesy of Direct Action Everywhere (DxE)" /> Earlier this year, I wrote at length about that practice

These wooden crates provide each calf about 13 square feet of living space, less than one-tenth the size of a typical parking spot. “We’re talking roughly the size of a coffin,” Vanessa Shakib, a lawyer and co-founder of the Los Angeles-area nonprofit Advancing Law for Animals , told me
Confining calves in this manner is not dissimilar to the use of gestation crates in the pork industry — tiny metal enclosures where pigs barely have room to move
Gestation crates have sparked intense national controversy that’s reached the halls of Congress and the US Supreme Court
But the extreme confinement of dairy calves has not received anywhere close to as much legal and political scrutiny.  In California, there’s an obvious legal problem with calf crates

The state has a plain-English law, Section 597t of its criminal code, that mandates that confined animals be provided an “adequate exercise area.” Though it doesn’t define what constitutes such an area, Shakib and other farm animal advocates argue that it strains credulity to believe the minuscule, barren crates provide one

The practice “is squarely at odds with the plain meaning of the words,” Shakib said.  But California has never enforced that law against calf crates in the state’s powerful dairy industry, where millions of newborn calves have been kept in extreme confinement (nor, apparently, has the law been enforced against any factory farm)

It’s a prime example of agricultural exceptionalism — the doctrine running through American legal and political culture, as Vox’s Kenny Torrella has written , that effectively absolves agribusiness from having to play by the same rules as everyone else.  Shakib and her organization are now hoping to change that.  They’re leading a lawsuit against Hettinga Dairy, a Southern California farm that has kept thousands of calves in individual crates, alleging that it’s violating Section 597t

If the case succeeds, it could create a blueprint for similar challenges statewide, and even spark a broader reckoning within America’s dairy industry.  The case that could transform how dairy calves are treated Advancing Law for Animals just filed suit on behalf of the Caru Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, a California animal protection nonprofit seeking a court ruling that the calf crates violate state law
The case names Hettinga Dairy and related defendants in connection with a  San Jacinto, California, facility that specializes in raising calves

The most recent available records from California’s State Water Resources Control Board report the farm’s animal population as 4,200 calves.  Such facilities, often known as “calf ranches” or “calf nurseries,” have become increasingly central to the US dairy business — as we wrote earlier this year, they “raise calves on dairy farms’ behalf during the fragile infant stage in which they’re too young to bring in any revenue.”  Caru SPCA (which is formerly known as the Animal Legal Defense Fund Cruelty Prevention Unit) flew drone cameras over the Hettinga facility earlier this year to document the calf housing there, filming the small wooden crates that are common in California and the Southwest, typically providing less than 15 square feet of space per calf

Many dairy farms and calf ranches use a different, plastic hutch design that provides more space, but the smaller wooden hutches remain widespread.  Calves typically spend about two months in these hutches before being moved into larger group pens; the lawsuit alleges that Hettinga keeps them in crates for around nine weeks.  “Calves are trapped for months, even in summer heat, unable to stretch their limbs or move freely,” the lawsuit alleges

Under 597t, “animals have a statutory right to minimal movement, and Defendants systematically violate that right daily, creating immense and ongoing suffering.” That San Jacinto farm is part of a broader network of dairy farms and calf-raising facilities linked to the Hettingas, a prominent dairy family whose farms collectively confine thousands of calves and cows across California, according to state public records
Most consumers have never heard of Hettinga, nor of the hundreds of other industrial dairies and calf-raising farms across California that operate largely out of public view
But the Hettingas also have a presence on grocery store shelves: According to the brand’s website, the family also owns Sarah Farms , a mass-market milk label in the Southwestern US
Vox emailed a list of questions about the allegations in the lawsuit to multiple contacts associated with Hettinga businesses
An employee at GH Processing , a Hettinga family-associated dairy plant in Arizona, confirmed receiving the email and said she would pass it on to colleagues in California

No one responded to Vox’s questions by publication time.  A representative from the California water board told Vox that the 2024 annual report for the San Jacinto calf facility identified Hein and Ellen Hettinga as the farm’s operators
But state regulators have not received the 2025 report, which was due in January 2026, and could not verify the facility’s current ownership

Hein Hettinga, who built the family’s dairy empire, died in 2023; Ellen, his wife, is one of the defendants named in the lawsuit.  Dairy industry trade groups often defend calf crates, arguing that they allow farmers to provide each animal with individualized care and reduce their exposure to pathogens

Whether that’s true is contested — some industry veterinarians endorse that view, while others maintain that it’s based on a narrow view of calves’ well-being and that properly managed social housing need not harm their physical health

Even within the industry, there’s growing acknowledgement that isolation is harmful to calves, and that it would be better for dairy farms to transition to a different system.  A 2023 assessment of calf welfare from the European Food Safety Authority — the EU agency that provides scientific guidance on animal welfare — found “no locomotor play behavior possible” for calves given a space allowance of about 16 square feet each
A calf in such confinement “is expected to spend most of its time lying down because no other activities can be performed,” the review states

To fully express natural behaviors like galloping, jumping, and kicking, it recommends that calves housed alone be allotted 318 square feet each, and calves housed in groups be allotted 215 square feet each, though it notes that even smaller increases in space could meaningfully improve their welfare.  Guidelines from Calf Care and Quality Assurance, a US industry-created animal care program, state that “individually housed calves have a harder time coping with changes in housing and diet and may have cognitive and developmental disadvantages, including poor learning skills and deficient social skills.” Temple Grandin, the famed livestock scientist at Colorado State University, has written that “calves should be raised with other calves, not in isolation.” They are, after all, intensely social herd animals.  Regardless of the industry’s opinion on the practice, though, 597t makes no exception for livestock industry standard practices, the way some states’ animal cruelty laws do. “It doesn’t matter whether this defendant or whether the dairy industry believes solitary confinement of baby animals serves a useful purpose,” Shakib said. “California law here is crystal clear — it requires an adequate exercise area

Industry custom or convenience does not erase that requirement.” California’s animal cruelty double standard The ubiquitous confinement of dairy calves in tiny crates remains poorly understood by the general public, and even, to some extent, within the animal protection movement
That is because, for many years, animal advocates focused their campaigning against extreme confinement in the dairy industry on veal, the notorious specialty meat made from male dairy calves

Those efforts helped bring about California’s Proposition 12, a landmark law passed in 2018 that bans certain forms of extreme confinement, including tiny crates that used to be the norm in veal production
Any veal raised or sold in California must now come from calves allotted at least 43 square feet of living space each

But the overwhelming share of California’s dairy calves are not raised for veal and thus get no protection under Prop 12, even as many members of the public may assume the problem of extreme confinement of calves has been solved.  In the last few years, however, a small wave of animal advocates have been drawing attention to the continued plight of dairy calves

The animal rights group Direct Action Everywhere (DxE) over the last year has documented and mapped calf confinement across California, including at Grimmius Cattle Company, the largest calf raiser in the state and the subject of Vox’s earlier reporting

This fall, DxE investigator Lewis Bernier obtained footage showing calves from a dairy farm that the group said supplies to Land O’Lakes being transported to Grimmius, where the newborn animals are raised in the same standard, approximately 13-square-foot wooden hutches

Land O’Lakes did not respond to requests for comment.  The crates aren’t the only problem Beyond extreme confinement in crates,  DxE’s investigations have surfaced allegations of overt abuse of calves — including animals being kicked, punched, and pulled by their ears and tails — at calf ranches and dairy farms throughout California

Drone footage taken earlier this year at a dairy farm that DxE linked to Leprino Foods — a major cheese supplier that reportedly sells to Domino’s, Papa John’s, and Pizza Hut, among others — shows calves being kicked, pushed, pulled by their ears, and thrown to the ground

title: Why the Nvidia CEO’s resignation is so important
excerpt: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, pictured at the Invest in Germany Summit on October 19, 2026 in Berlin. | Thomas Koehler/Photothek via Getty Images Editor’s note,
body: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, pictured at the Invest in Germany Summit on October 19, 2026 in Berlin. | Thomas Koehler/Photothek via Getty Images Editor’s note, November 12, 3:35 pm ET: This story was originally posted on November 9 and is being republished today in light of Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO

The movie version of Jensen Huang’s jaw-dropping affair basically writes itself.  Cast BD Wong as 63-year-old Huang, the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies and a close friend of President Donald Trump

Kelly Hu can play Alice Huang, Jensen’s paramour and — even better — a purported agent of the Chinese government.  The role of Trump himself, who reportedly knew about Huang’s undercover girlfriend but on Sunday said Huang “probably has an excuse for it,” can be played by Alec Baldwin. (Or a flightless duck — your pick.) However you cast it, this whole sordid affair has “serialized Netflix drama” written all over it
But in all seriousness…the possibility that one of the world’s most powerful men was targeted by Chinese intelligence is a big deal on multiple scores
Nvidia has opened its own investigation into whether Huang was compromised, and congressional leaders have requested he brief them in a closed-door session

Nvidia supplies much of the computing power behind the AI boom, giving it enormous influence over the broader economy. “If they sneeze, everybody else catches a cold,” the writer and economic commentator Kyla Scanlon told Vox’s Today, Explained podcast last year
That makes this whole episode a little more weighty than your standard billionaire’s affair
Go a little deeper View Link Nvidia is the most valuable company on Earth — but in many households, it’s still not a household name

Huang and two other electrical engineers founded the now-$4.5-trillion company in 1993 with the fairly niche and nerdy goal of making high-powered chips that could render the 3D graphics for a new generation of video games.  Then, in 2006, the company released software tools that let programmers use its chips for other demanding computing tasks, like mining cryptocurrency and training AI models
When companies like OpenAI began developing tools like ChatGPT, they immediately turned to Nvidia.  That made the company a cornerstone of America’s AI buildout and a major economic force
In 2024, Nvidia alone accounted for more than a fifth of the S&P 500’s total return
And the rush to build out AI infrastructure has accounted for much of America’s recent economic growth , according to St
Nvidia’s influence  extends to the White House, too , where Huang is a regular guest of Trump

The two became fast friends after having dinner together at Mar-a-Lago last year, and Huang has said Trump regularly calls him late at night to discuss topics like “protecting national security” and “creating more jobs.”  But Huang’s ambitions have run up against one major obstacle: US restrictions on selling Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China
US officials worry that their enormous computing power could help Beijing develop weapons, strengthen its military, expand surveillance, and otherwise rival US military and technological dominance
That helps explain why China (allegedly) sicced a spy on Huang: They really want these chips

The New York Times reports that China’s top intelligence agency recruited Alice Huang both to learn more about America’s advanced chip industry and to potentially influence Nvidia’s push to lift export restrictions

Alice Huang, it should be noted, was a data center executive in her own right, and her company  has been investigated for purportedly helping to smuggle Nvidia chips into China.  All these investigations will hopefully, eventually, reveal whether their affair compromised anything beyond Huang’s marriage
They may also test how dependent Nvidia is on his leadership.  With Huang out as CEO, uncertainty over the company’s future could unsettle investors and trigger wobbles in the wider market
That’s the problem with concentrating so much power in any one person or company: One person’s (very) personal business can somehow become everybody’s problem.  One link for later ➨ Get a hobby
But not just any hobby: something that’s intentionally imperfect, unproductive or unquantified
There’s a tendency in American culture to try to optimize or commodify our leisure , the writer Jenny Odell explains
But that undermines some of leisure’s biggest benefits — like cultivating a sense of joy, wonder, or learning
Before you go… Did you know… that Alexander Graham Bell reportedly wanted people to answer the phone with a cheerful “ahoy” ? Alas, Thomas Edison’s preferred greeting — “hello” — won out instead
Today’s trivia: Cleopatra was killed by what animal, according to several contemporaneous accounts? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for Ricky Martin’s biggest hit

That would be “ Livin’ La Vida Loca ,” the 1999 bop that’s widely credited with launching the Latin pop explosion of the late 1990s and early 2000s.   This post intially appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here .

title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
excerpt: Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats Two skulls, including that of a man believed to
body: Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century

One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities

title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
excerpt: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming thresh
body: A charged atmosphere in Antalya: COP31 is unfolding against a backdrop of war, spiking energy prices, and a world already blowing past the 1.5 °C warming threshold the Paris Agreement was designed to prevent
The money problem: Rich nations promised $300 billion a year by 2035 for climate action, but delivered less than half that in 2024

Fossil fuels back in the spotlight: After last year's final agreement didn't mention "fossil fuels" once, expect a fight over language—especially with cohosts Australia and Turkey both deeply tied to coal and gas. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148308" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey
COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world
Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20
This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis
And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular

Here’s what you should know about COP31.   In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked
This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US
President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change

That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.  Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels

In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming

There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.  Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas
The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage
The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country)
Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels
Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them
But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once

This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal
Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching

These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.   One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go
The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there
The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use
Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity
Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest
Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions

The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.  With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change
I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.  To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death
Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud
Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine

MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits
Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk
Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify
The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models
Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology
The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems

title: Evolving metal extraction processes
excerpt: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting
body: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible
Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago
Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence

According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience
That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments

Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions
Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control
EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways
The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production
Laboratory work revealed broader potential
Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions
They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed
The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness

Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology Source : Outokumpu Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world

Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT. “The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore
Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches

The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste

Innovation happens at the boundaries EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies
Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering

With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work. “Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn
Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production
Building a technology platform A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform
Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications
Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources
The initial application becomes only the starting point. “The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing
The future of materials companies The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy
Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives
The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027
The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030
Beyond producing low-CO 2 , chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum

The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today? The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on
Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore
